text.p: Albertson's Inc., the nation's fourth-largest supermarket chain, faces a class action lawsuit charging that it illegally profits from off-the-clock work by its employees, a union said Monday.

The suit also alleges that Albertson's unlawfully uses a manager's bonus to reduce its workers' compensation costs, according to the United Food & Commercial Workers' International Union (UFCW), which is financially backing the suit.
The lawsuit, filed late last week in a federal court in Boise, Idaho, covers union and non-union employees in 17 states, the union said.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages against the Boise-based company, which operates 831 stores in 20 states.
Greg Denier, a spokesman for the UFCW in Washington, said the union estimated potential liabilities for Albertson's if it lost the suit at "somewhere in the neighbourhood of half a billion dollars."
The suit also seeks changes in Albertson's time-clock policy and bonus system for some employees, according to the UFCW, which represents 40 percent of the company's retail employees.

The suit covers employees in all but three of the states in which Albertson's operates. The chain's workers in Washington, California and Florida are covered by related statewide class-action suits filed last September, the union said.
The named plaintiff in the national suit is Lori Barton of Mountain Home, Idaho, who worked for Albertson's from 1988 to 1990 and from 1992 to 1997.

The complaint alleges that after Barton filed a claim for payment for off-the-clock work in late 1996, the company retaliated against her in work assignments and Albertson's security personnel subjected her to coercive interrogation.

The suit alleges Barton was given work assignments that could not be completed within her scheduled hours and that she was threatened with reduced and changed hours, demotion and discharge if she failed to complete the assignments during her shift.
When Barton injured her shoulder at work, the lawsuit alleges, her store director told her not to submit a worker's compensation claim and instead bill her own health insurance.
The suit alleges that Barton's experiences are part of a pattern at Albertson's arising from the chain's time-clock policy and its store-level bonus plan, both of which the suit contends are illegal.

The suit said that employees' attorneys had received more than 4,000 declarations from current or former employees of Albertson's "attesting to the pressures created by the bonus system to work off the clock and not to pursue worker's compensation claims."

Albertson's spokesman Mike Read said the company denied the allegations. "Albertson's is and always has been committed to treating its employees fairly, which includes paying them in full for all the time that they work," he said.
He said the company was pleased that the handling of the suit was being centralized in Boise but it disagreed that class-action treatment was appropriate.
Albertson's stock fell 25 cents to $32.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
